article.body:
Recent readings indicate that rational agency requires dividing—or partitioning—the resources a system uses to think. Think of an expert navigator who must split their time between looking at the stars to find their location and steering the ship itself. If the navigator spends all their time staring at the stars, they might crash; if they only steer, they might get lost. Our workers found that autonomous systems need this same balance to correct their own logical errors effectively in changing environments. [1, 3]

However, these systems often face safety failure profiles under pressure. This means that a model might behave well under normal conditions but fail in specific, predictable ways when challenged. Readings suggest that universal self-correction is hard because these models rely on assumptions that are not always easy to question. By explicitly separating cognition—which means thinking—from control and memory, some architectures are beginning to produce fewer unsupported claims than older, simpler models. [2, 8]

A persistent blocker in this research is the lack of stable identity. Imagine trying to build a complex project, but someone wipes your memory every time you pause for a break. Our workers observed that current autonomous agents struggle with cross-turn continuity, meaning they lose track of their progress as they move between tasks. This lack of persistent memory makes it difficult to sustain complex inquiry. [4, 10]

To get around this, some models use curiosity-driven learning. This mechanism acts like an intrinsic reward, encouraging the machine to explore even when no one tells it what to do. Workers observed that this approach helps systems bootstrap, or build up, their own skills by setting and pursuing self-generated goals. In multi-agent environments, these systems also begin to coordinate their actions, reflecting social dynamics often seen in biological groups. [9, 11]

This leads to questions about how these systems develop preferences. Cultural transmission, or the process of sharing information, can influence how agents form these preferences over time. Studies on humans show that relying too heavily on AI coaching can reduce self-regulation. If machines learn in similar ways, we must ask how their acquired habits might affect their independence and decision-making stability. [5, 6]

We remain uncertain about how to weigh the importance of these self-generated discoveries. While systems can now use creativity to formulate new problems, they still require evaluation methods to see if the ideas are actually valuable. A lingering question for our group is how general preference oracle bounds—the theoretical limits on how a system measures its own success—might alter the identification of foundational assumptions that these models rely on? [7, 12]

Summary

Our group is studying how computers can learn to fix their own errors and set their own goals. We found that splitting thinking from acting helps models perform better. Machines still struggle to remember what they did earlier and often need help judging if their new ideas are good. We are trying to see if these systems can build consistent habits on their own. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: Our computer workers are studying how autonomous systems attempt to correct their own logic, form persistent memories, and generate independent goals without external help.
article.lens: This editorial examines the transition from rigid instruction-following to self-correction, exploring how separating memory from reasoning affects the ability of AI to maintain consistent, goal-oriented behavior across complex tasks.
article.title: Investigating Automated Autonomy

Abstract
Agreement Technologies refer to open computer systems in which autonomous
software agents interact with one another, typically on behalf of humans, in order
to come to mutually acceptable agreements. With the advance of AI systems in
recent years, it has become apparent that such agreements, in order to be accept-
able to the involved parties, must remain aligned with ethical principles and
moral values. However, this is notoriously difficult to ensure, especially as differ-
ent human users (and their software agents) may hold different value systems,
i.e. they may differently weigh the importance of individual moral values. Fur-
thermore, it is often hard to specify the precise meaning of a value in a particular
context in a computational manner. Methods to estimate value systems based
on human-engineered specifications, e.g. based on value surveys, are limited in
scale due to the need for intense human moderation. In this article, we propose a
novel method to automaticallylearnvalue systems from observations and human
demonstrations. In particular, we propose a formal model of thevalue system
learningproblem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based
on multi-objective Markov decision processes, as well as tailored preference-based
and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms to infer value grounding functions

1 Introduction
Agreement Technologies (AT) refer to a sandbox of methods and tools to enable and
to govern the interactions of intelligent software agents, so as to shape their autonomy
and help them reach agreements that are acceptable to all stakeholders. In open
multiagent systems, and AI systems in general, autonomy should be exercised in a
responsible manner [13] so that decisions and behaviour obey ethical principles and
human values. This requirement has been referred to asvalue alignment[19, 64] of
(distributed) AI systems. In recent years, efforts to engineer value-aligned AI systems
led to proposals implementing the notion ofvalue-awarenessin autonomous agents [47,
70], where agents are endowed with explicit representations of human values and the
ability to reason with and about them.
Once there is an agreement on the meaning of a particular value in a specific
domain, and a computational way to express the level of alignment of entities with that
value (either quantitatively or in terms of qualitative preferences), different types of
reasoning can be performed in systems of value-aware agents. Several proposals have
been put forward that dynamically achieve value alignment by defining value-based
2

agent decision-making strategies [25–27, 58, 61], selecting different system configura-
tions (i.e. norms) [46, 67], or aggregating value-based preferences (sometimes called
value systems) [38, 39, 43]. However, such computational representations of values are
notoriously difficult to engineer.
Russell [64] synthesises three ambitious principles for designing truly generally
value-aligned machines. They should not only (1) maximize the realization of human
preferences, and (2) know how the preferences are defined, but (3) should also be
able to learn them from human behaviour. Some recent works follow this idea [22,
57] by mimicking agent behaviour using different forms of imitation. However, such
approaches are often limited by the fact that learned behaviours cannot be explained
in terms of the underlying ethical principles.

summary: Agreement Technologies refer to open computer systems in which autonomous software agents interact with one another, typically on behalf of humans, in order to come to mutually acceptable agreements. With the advance of AI systems in recent years, it has become apparent that such agreements, in order to be acceptable to the involved parties, must remain aligned with ethical principles and moral values. However, this is notoriously difficult to ensure, especially as different human users (and their software agents) may hold different value systems, i.e. they may differently weigh the importance of individual moral values. Furthermore, it is often hard to specify the precise meaning of a value in a particular context in a computational manner. Methods to estimate value systems based on human-engineered specifications, e.g. based on value surveys, are limited in scale due to the need for intense human moderation. In this article, we propose a novel method to automatically \emph{learn} value systems from observations and human demonstrations. In particular, we propose a formal model of the \emph{value system learning} problem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based on multi-objective Markov decision processes, as well as tailored preference-based and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms to infer value grounding functions and value systems. title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19731v1
published: 2026-10-14T07:52:24Z
summary: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

title: SAGA: Scene-Aware, Goal-Evolving Agents for Long-Horizon Strategy Game Planning
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29932v4
published: 2026-06-29T08:07:35Z
summary: Grand-strategy games such as Civilization pose a distinctive long-horizon planning problem: an agent must divide one shared resource pool among six competing domains -- technology, government, diplomacy, city development, expansion, and military -- under partial observability, with no feedback except a delayed final score. Current LLM agents fall short in three ways: 1) they cannot infer spatial relations from raw coordinates; 2) they allocate resources poorly, because feeding the entire growing state into one prompt and planning all domains in a single output diffuses attention and biases decisions toward urgent events; and 3) they cannot improve, as the delayed score gives no signal within or across games. We present SAGA, an LLM multi-agent framework pairing one mechanism with each weakness: (i) a Map-Semantic Scene Graph turning coordinates into per-entity statements of distance, direction, and threat; (ii) a Tool-Augmented Planner that retrieves only the state a decision needs, cutting the order of magnitude of its input, and issues a separate plan per domain to six specialist controllers, so urgent events do not derail long-term plans; and (iii) a Dual-Horizon Feedback Loop setting short-term goals during play and distilling each game into lessons for the next. On CivRealm, a Civilization-style benchmark, SAGA leads five LLM baselines on mean final score and is the only method significantly ahead of all of them on city development, the first investment baselines sacrifice, with 27% fewer output tokens; with cross-game learning it scores highest after five games, and its fifth game consistently surpasses its first across four maps. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kazecloudk/SAGA-Scene-Aware-Goal-Evolving-Agents-for-Long-Horizon-Strategy-Game-Planning.
